body:
### Process detection logic triplicated across all three plugins **Medium Severity** The tmux TTY → `ps` lookup → PID check logic (~45 lines) is copy-pasted across all three agent plugins, differing only in a hardcoded process name string (`"aider"`, `"codex"`, `"claude"`). Each agent already exposes a `processName` property with this value, so a shared parameterized helper (e.g. in core or a shared utils module) could replace all three copies. A bug fix or platform compatibility change to this subprocess logic would need to be applied in three places.
Additional Locations (2) - [`packages/plugins/agent-codex/src/index.ts#L82-L128`](https://github.com/ComposioHQ/agent-orchestrator/blob/ce9ee17c4901cf595b168c6fc6b4e7d2d775dc61/packages/plugins/agent-codex/src/index.ts#L82-L128) - [`packages/plugins/agent-claude-code/src/index.ts#L247-L298`](https://github.com/ComposioHQ/agent-orchestrator/blob/ce9ee17c4901cf595b168c6fc6b4e7d2d775dc61/packages/plugins/agent-claude-code/src/index.ts#L247-L298)

### Shell escape utility duplicated across all three plugins **Low Severity** The `shellEscape` function is identically defined in all three agent plugins. Since all three packages already depend on `@agent-orchestrator/core`, this utility could live there (or in a shared utils module) to avoid maintaining three copies.
Additional Locations (2) - [`packages/plugins/agent-codex/src/index.ts#L33-L36`](https://github.com/ComposioHQ/agent-orchestrator/blob/ce9ee17c4901cf595b168c6fc6b4e7d2d775dc61/packages/plugins/agent-codex/src/index.ts#L33-L36) - [`packages/plugins/agent-claude-code/src/index.ts#L205-L208`](https://github.com/ComposioHQ/agent-orchestrator/blob/ce9ee17c4901cf595b168c6fc6b4e7d2d775dc61/packages/plugins/agent-claude-code/src/index.ts#L205-L208)

### Polling skips runtime death transitions **Medium Severity** `pollAll()` filters out sessions already marked `killed` by `sessionManager.list()`, so dead-runtime sessions never reach `checkSession()`. That prevents `lifecycle-manager.ts` from emitting `session.killed`, updating metadata via `updateMetadata`, and running any reaction logic for that transition during normal polling.
Additional Locations (1) - [`packages/core/src/session-manager.ts#L303-L306`](https://github.com/ComposioHQ/agent-orchestrator/blob/20693f742ddff830b2c58fb994bb1e744621f9c1/packages/core/src/session-manager.ts#L303-L306)

### Reaction retries bypassed on first send failure **Medium Severity** In `executeReaction()`, a `send-to-agent` failure immediately calls `notifyHuman()` and returns `escalated: true`, even when `ReactionConfig.retries` allows more attempts. This makes `retries` ineffective for transient `sessionManager.send()` failures.

### Successful reactions still trigger escalation limits **Medium Severity** `executeReaction()` increments `tracker.attempts` before execution and uses it for escalation, but never resets it after success. This makes `retries` behave like total event count, so later successful `send-to-agent` reactions can be escalated even without prior failures.

### Spawn failures leak runtime and workspace **High Severity** After `runtime.create()` succeeds, failures in `writeMetadata()` or `agent.postLaunchSetup()` are not rolled back. `spawn()` throws but leaves the runtime session and workspace alive, creating orphaned resources and inconsistent state with no session metadata.
Additional Locations (1) - [`packages/core/src/session-manager.ts#L228-L235`](https://github.com/ComposioHQ/agent-orchestrator/blob/20693f742ddff830b2c58fb994bb1e744621f9c1/packages/core/src/session-manager.ts#L228-L235)

### Kill omits cleanup when project config missing **Medium Severity** `kill()` only destroys runtime/workspace when `config.projects[projectId]` exists. If a session references a removed or renamed project, it skips destruction and still calls `deleteMetadata()`, leaving the actual runtime/workspace running but removing the only tracking record.
Additional Locations (1) - [`packages/core/src/session-manager.ts#L359-L361`](https://github.com/ComposioHQ/agent-orchestrator/blob/20693f742ddff830b2c58fb994bb1e744621f9c1/packages/core/src/session-manager.ts#L359-L361)

### Shell injection via unescaped single quotes in printf **High Severity** The `printf` command in the `write text` AppleScript uses `${safe}` (AppleScript-escaped only) inside a shell single-quoted context. `escapeAppleScript` only handles backslashes and double quotes — it does not escape single quotes. If the session name contains a `'`, it breaks out of the shell single-quoted string, leading to command injection. The `tmux attach` part correctly uses `${shellSafe}`, but the `printf` part does not.

### Duplicated `escapeAppleScript` across two plugin packages **Low Severity** `escapeAppleScript` is defined identically in both `notifier-desktop` and `terminal-iterm2`. Duplicating this security-sensitive escaping logic increases the risk that a future bug fix is applied to one copy but not the other. Extracting it into a shared utility (or the `@agent-orchestrator/core` package) would ensure consistent behavior.
Additional Locations (1) - [`packages/plugins/notifier-desktop/src/index.ts#L21-L24`](https://github.com/ComposioHQ/agent-orchestrator/blob/eccbbe1f2f935b14b66fd7a9ea10b5d5e07974f1/packages/plugins/notifier-desktop/src/index.ts#L21-L24)

### Attention level misclassifies sessions with `reviewDecision: "none"` **High Severity** `getAttentionLevel` only checks `pr.reviewDecision === "pending"` for the warning zone, but `"none"` is also a "needs review" state. Both `getAlerts` in `SessionCard` and `getMockStats` correctly handle `"pending" || "none"`, but `getAttentionLevel` omits `"none"`. This causes sessions like `frontend-5` (annotated as `// WARNING`) to land in the "ok" zone instead of "warning", while still displaying a "needs review" alert tag and being counted in the stats bar's "need review" number.
Additional Locations (2) - [`packages/web/src/components/SessionCard.tsx#L277-L278`](https://github.com/ComposioHQ/agent-orchestrator/blob/a58f3dd6008b6e61f9b09797a547e3ec3354110c/packages/web/src/components/SessionCard.tsx#L277-L278) - [`packages/web/src/lib/mock-data.ts#L409-L410`](https://github.com/ComposioHQ/agent-orchestrator/blob/a58f3dd6008b6e61f9b09797a547e3ec3354110c/packages/web/src/lib/mock-data.ts#L409-L410)

### ACTION zone uses green color instead of orange **Medium Severity** The PR spec defines the color scheme as "ACTION (orange)" but the `action` zone config in `AttentionZone` uses `var(--color-accent-green)` and `borderColorByLevel` in `SessionCard` uses `border-l-[var(--color-accent-green)]`. This makes the ACTION zone visually indistinguishable in meaning from a "success" state, undermining the attention-zone priority signaling.
Additional Locations (1) - [`packages/web/src/components/SessionCard.tsx#L26-L27`](https://github.com/ComposioHQ/agent-orchestrator/blob/a58f3dd6008b6e61f9b09797a547e3ec3354110c/packages/web/src/components/SessionCard.tsx#L26-L27)

### SessionDetail date rendering causes hydration mismatch **Medium Severity** `SessionDetail` calls `new Date(session.createdAt).toLocaleString()` directly in the render body for the "Created" and "Last Activity" info cards. Since this is a `"use client"` component, it's still server-rendered initially, and `toLocaleString()` produces locale/timezone-dependent output. In production, where server and client locales differ, this creates a React hydration mismatch. The `Dashboard` component explicitly avoids this exact problem with a `ClientTimestamp` pattern using `useState` + `useEffect`, but that pattern wasn't applied here.

### SSE route missing dynamic export will be cached **High Severity** The SSE endpoint `GET` handler takes no `Request` parameter and the file has no `export const dynamic = "force-dynamic"` declaration. In Next.js App Router, GET route handlers without a `Request` parameter are treated as static and cached by default. This means the streaming response will be evaluated once and cached — the SSE endpoint won't create a fresh stream per client, completely breaking real-time event delivery. Every Next.js SSE tutorial shows this directive as required.

### Process name substring match causes false positives **Medium Severity** The condition `args.includes("/claude")` performs a substring match, so it falsely matches any process whose path contains `/claude` as a prefix — e.g., `/usr/bin/claude-desktop`, `/path/to/claudette`. This can cause `isProcessRunning` and `detectActivity` to incorrectly report a dead session as alive. The same issue affects the aider (`/aider`) and codex (`/codex`) plugins. Using `args.endsWith("/processName")` instead of `args.includes("/processName")` would fix the false-positive matching. Note that `args.includes("/claude ")` (condition 3) is also fully redundant since it's a subset of `args.includes("/claude")` (condition 4).
Additional Locations (2) - [`packages/plugins/agent-aider/src/index.ts#L101-L107`](https://github.com/ComposioHQ/agent-orchestrator/blob/0be565ae9994c05a9f1814537cbad817756a708b/packages/plugins/agent-aider/src/index.ts#L101-L107) - [`packages/plugins/agent-codex/src/index.ts#L105-L111`](https://github.com/ComposioHQ/agent-orchestrator/blob/0be565ae9994c05a9f1814537cbad817756a708b/packages/plugins/agent-codex/src/index.ts#L105-L111)

### Reactions never retry without state changes **High Severity** `executeReaction()` is only invoked inside the status-transition branch, so reactions run once when status first changes and never run again while the status stays the same. This prevents configured retry counting and time-based escalation in `lifecycle-manager.ts` for persistent states like `ci_failed` or `changes_requested`.
Additional Locations (1) - [`packages/core/src/lifecycle-manager.ts#L397-L407`](https://github.com/ComposioHQ/agent-orchestrator/blob/25826c0be3e8187b26a605587abe8036061f2bb1/packages/core/src/lifecycle-manager.ts#L397-L407)

### Blocked sessions cannot recover to working **Medium Severity** When `agent.detectActivity()` returns active/idle and no PR state overrides apply, `determineStatus()` returns `session.status` (except `spawning`). Sessions in `needs_input` or `stuck` therefore remain pinned to those states even after the agent resumes normal activity.

### Project reaction overrides drop default fields **High Severity** `project.reactions` entries are `Partial`, but `checkSession()` uses them as full replacements via `??` instead of merging with `config.reactions`. If a project override sets only one field like `auto`, required fields like `action` can disappear, causing the reaction to never execute.

### Spawning without workspace breaks isolation **High Severity** `spawn()` validates `runtime` and `agent` plugins but not `workspace`. If `workspace` is unavailable, it silently uses `project.path` as `workspacePath`, so sessions run in the main repo instead of isolated workspaces. This can cause concurrent sessions to interfere with each other and persist unsafe metadata for later cleanup.
Additional Locations (1) - [`packages/core/src/session-manager.ts#L175-L191`](https://github.com/ComposioHQ/agent-orchestrator/blob/25826c0be3e8187b26a605587abe8036061f2bb1/packages/core/src/session-manager.ts#L175-L191)

### AppleScript injection via unescaped session name in shell command **High Severity** The `shellSafe` variable (from `shellEscape`) is interpolated into an AppleScript double-quoted string without AppleScript escaping. `shellEscape` only handles single quotes for shell safety, so a session name containing `"` (e.g., from `runtimeHandle.id` or `session.id`) would break the AppleScript string delimiter in the `write text` command, enabling AppleScript injection. The `safe` variable is correctly escaped for AppleScript, but `shellSafe` needs both shell escaping *and* AppleScript escaping — applying `escapeAppleScript(shellEscape(sessionName))` would handle the layered quoting correctly.
Additional Locations (1) - [`packages/plugins/terminal-iterm2/src/index.ts#L98-L99`](https://github.com/ComposioHQ/agent-orchestrator/blob/dea051b3bc56ffa181cc77c5f5c9b921a834d3c7/packages/plugins/terminal-iterm2/src/index.ts#L98-L99)

 

Triggered by project rule: BugBot Configuration

### Default dashboard port inconsistent with core config **Medium Severity** The default `dashboardUrl` uses port 9847 (`http://localhost:9847`), but the core config schema in `config.ts` defaults the dashboard port to 3000. This means terminal URLs generated by this plugin will point to the wrong port when using defaults, producing broken links that fail to connect.

### Falsy check conflates empty stdout with command failure **High Severity** The `git()` helper returns stdout on success and `null` on failure. Since `git worktree add -b` writes output to stderr (not stdout), a successful command returns an empty string `""`. The check `if (!result)` treats empty string as falsy, so the code always enters the fallback "branch already exists" path even when the first command succeeded. This triggers a second `git worktree add` that fails (worktree path already exists) and is silently swallowed. The correct check is `if (result === null)`.

### Shell injection via bash -c with interpolated string **Medium Severity** Calling `exec("bash", ["-c", ...])` with an interpolated `tty` variable inside a shell command string bypasses the security benefit of `execFile`. Although `tty` comes from tmux output and is typically safe, this pattern violates the project's security rule to prefer `execFile` over `exec` and avoid string concatenation in shell commands. The `tty` value is embedded in a double-quoted context inside a `bash -c` string, which could allow command injection if the value contained shell metacharacters.

 

Triggered by project rule: BugBot Configuration

### Batch-spawn duplicate detection uses stale tmux session list **Medium Severity** In `batch-spawn`, `allTmux` is captured once before the loop, but `findSessionForIssue` requires matching sessions to be in the `tmuxSessions` list (line 73 of `metadata.ts`). Newly spawned sessions within the same batch write metadata to disk but aren't in the stale `allTmux` list, so `findSessionForIssue` skips them during the `tmuxSessions.includes(name)` check. This means duplicate issue IDs passed in the same batch won't be detected, potentially spawning multiple sessions for the same issue.
Additional Locations (1) - [`packages/cli/src/lib/metadata.ts#L70-L73`](https://github.com/ComposioHQ/agent-orchestrator/blob/cc11b3ec596be3b3ddd471f8eec3ee74ce742dc3/packages/cli/src/lib/metadata.ts#L70-L73)

### Substring matching causes false-positive duplicate issue detection **Medium Severity** `findSessionForIssue` uses `meta.issue.toLowerCase().includes(lower)` for matching, which is substring-based rather than exact equality. Searching for issue `"INT-1"` would false-positive match a session with issue `"INT-10"`, `"INT-100"`, or `"INT-12"`, since `"int-10".includes("int-1")` is `true`. This causes `batch-spawn` to incorrectly skip spawning sessions for legitimate new issues, silently reporting them as duplicates.

### Missing project validation crashes session ls and cleanup **Medium Severity** The `session ls` and `session cleanup` subcommands are missing the unknown-project validation that `status` and `review-check` have. When `--project nonexistent` is passed, `config.projects[opts.project]` is `undefined`, making the `projects` map contain `{ "nonexistent": undefined }`. Iterating it and accessing `project.sessionPrefix` on `undefined` throws an unhandled `TypeError`, crashing the CLI.
Additional Locations (1) - [`packages/cli/src/commands/session.ts#L118-L129`](https://github.com/ComposioHQ/agent-orchestrator/blob/cc11b3ec596be3b3ddd471f8eec3ee74ce742dc3/packages/cli/src/commands/session.ts#L118-L129)

### `getPendingComments` returns resolved comments too **Medium Severity** The `SCM` interface documents `getPendingComments` as returning "pending (unresolved) review comments," but the implementation's `.filter()` only excludes bot authors — it never checks `t.isResolved`. All non-bot review threads are returned regardless of resolution status, violating the interface contract and potentially causing the orchestrator to treat already-resolved comments as outstanding work items.

### Duplicated `gh` helper across two plugin packages **Low Severity** The `gh` helper function (wrapping `execFileAsync` with identical error handling, timeout, and buffer config) is copy-pasted verbatim between `scm-github` and `tracker-github`. Maintaining two identical copies increases the risk of divergent bug fixes or inconsistent behavior when one copy is updated but not the other.
Additional Locations (1) - [`packages/plugins/tracker-github/src/index.ts#L24-L37`](https://github.com/ComposioHQ/agent-orchestrator/blob/ae0eccdde9d8208ceb67fc26fd48fa62bb2ba084/packages/plugins/tracker-github/src/index.ts#L24-L37)

### Non-tmux runtimes return "idle" instead of "active" **Medium Severity** `detectActivity` returns `"idle"` for non-tmux runtimes (where `output` stays `null`), but returns `"active"` when tmux `capture-pane` throws an error. Both situations mean "process confirmed alive, no terminal output available," yet they produce different results. The `"idle"` state semantically means "agent is at prompt, waiting for input," which is an incorrect assertion when output simply isn't accessible. The `!output` null check was designed for the empty-tmux-pane case but inadvertently catches the non-tmux case too.
Additional Locations (1) - [`packages/plugins/agent-claude-code/src/index.ts#L374-L378`](https://github.com/ComposioHQ/agent-orchestrator/blob/cf09b9b8c629d0a69e2900b10d425324a0753c06/packages/plugins/agent-claude-code/src/index.ts#L374-L378)

### Unguarded JSON.parse cast to JsonlLine type **Low Severity** `JSON.parse(trimmed) as JsonlLine` casts the parsed result without validating its shape. If a JSONL line contains a bare `null`, the cast hides the mismatch from TypeScript. Downstream in `extractCost`, accessing `line.costUSD` or `line.usage` on `null` would throw a `TypeError`, unlike `extractSummary` and `extractLastMessageType` which use optional chaining (`line?.type`). This violates the project rule about unguarded `JSON.parse`.

 

Triggered by project rule: BugBot Configuration

### Reaction escalation counts successful attempts **Medium Severity** `executeReaction()` increments `tracker.attempts` before execution and uses it for escalation regardless of outcome. Successful `send-to-agent` runs still increase retry counters, so repeated re-entry into the same state can escalate to human notifications even when auto-handling keeps succeeding.
Additional Locations (1) - [`packages/core/src/lifecycle-manager.ts#L290-L305`](https://github.com/ComposioHQ/agent-orchestrator/blob/580cebe63f4f0ba158fa84a598beca656da2a3c5/packages/core/src/lifecycle-manager.ts#L290-L305)

### WORKING zone uses blue instead of specified green **Medium Severity** The `ok` (WORKING) zone's color is set to `var(--color-accent-blue)` but both the PR description and the architecture design doc (`artifacts/architecture-design.md` line 527: "**Green zone**: Sessions working normally") specify green. The color for the WORKING zone needs to be `var(--color-accent-green)` to match the design spec: URGENT=red, ACTION=orange, WARNING=yellow, WORKING=green, COMPLETED=grey.

### Redundant ternary always returns same value **Low Severity** The expression `session.pr ? "action" : "action"` in `getAttentionLevel` returns `"action"` in both branches, making the ternary dead logic. This looks like an incomplete implementation — perhaps the intent was to return a different level (like `"warning"` or `"ok"`) when there's no PR data for a session with `"mergeable"`/`"approved"` status.

### SSEEvent type is unused and structurally incorrect **Low Severity** The exported `SSEEvent` interface is never imported or referenced anywhere in the codebase. Additionally, its shape (`sessionId`, `priority`, `message`, `data` fields) doesn't match the actual SSE events produced by `/api/events/route.ts`, which emit `snapshot` events (with `sessions` array) and `session.activity` events (with `attentionLevel`, `timestamp`). This dead type with a wrong shape could mislead future consumers.

### Session ID not validated in kill and send routes **Medium Severity** The `id` URL parameter in the kill and send routes is used without validation. The spawn route validates user inputs with `validateIdentifier` (restricting to `[a-zA-Z0-9_-]+`), but the session routes accept arbitrary strings. When wired to core services that execute shell commands (e.g., `tmux kill-session`), unsanitized session IDs could enable command injection.
Additional Locations (1) - [`packages/web/src/app/api/sessions/[id]/send/route.ts#L7-L9`](https://github.com/ComposioHQ/agent-orchestrator/blob/04063f6f2b19c474c0b4c1bdd5ac4aa55438721d/packages/web/src/app/api/sessions/[id]/send/route.ts#L7-L9)

 

Triggered by project rule: BugBot Configuration

### PR discovery never happens from SCM **High Severity** `determineStatus()` only evaluates PR/CI/review logic when `session.pr` already exists. It never calls `scm.detectPR()`, so sessions that open a PR after spawn stay in `working` and never transition to `pr_open`/CI/review states unless metadata is updated elsewhere.
Additional Locations (1) - [`packages/core/src/types.ts#L344-L346`](https://github.com/ComposioHQ/agent-orchestrator/blob/c9480255e727d815b7a012f547638ca08707c549/packages/core/src/types.ts#L344-L346)

### Summary events get wrong default priority **Low Severity** `inferPriority()` treats any event type containing `completed` as `action`. This causes `summary.all_complete` events created in `lifecycle-manager.ts` to default to `action` instead of `info`, which misclassifies completion summaries in event history and any consumers that rely on event priority.
Additional Locations (1) - [`packages/core/src/lifecycle-manager.ts#L440-L446`](https://github.com/ComposioHQ/agent-orchestrator/blob/c9480255e727d815b7a012f547638ca08707c549/packages/core/src/lifecycle-manager.ts#L440-L446)

### Conflict and bot reactions never trigger **Medium Severity** `eventToReactionKey` defines reactions for `automated_review.found` and `merge.conflicts`, but `determineStatus` never checks `scm.getAutomatedComments` or conflict blockers and never emits those events. The configured `bugbot-comments` and `merge-conflicts` auto-reactions are therefore unreachable during lifecycle polling.
Additional Locations (1) - [`packages/core/src/lifecycle-manager.ts#L92-L96`](https://github.com/ComposioHQ/agent-orchestrator/blob/c26ed77b0b5e3fb5fe473e5235d10dc4544219bc/packages/core/src/lifecycle-manager.ts#L92-L96)

### Branch checkout arguments are in wrong mode **High Severity** `git checkout` is invoked with `--` in a position that switches parsing to path mode, so branch checkout logic is incorrect. In `workspace-clone`, `create` tries `checkout -b --` and then `checkout --`, which prevents normal branch creation/checkout. The same fallback pattern appears in `workspace-worktree`.
Additional Locations (1) - [`packages/plugins/workspace-worktree/src/index.ts#L73-L74`](https://github.com/ComposioHQ/agent-orchestrator/blob/16d7efb873c138fc04b50c31a3455233ac239429/packages/plugins/workspace-worktree/src/index.ts#L73-L74)

### Stale spawn error handler deletes live process **High Severity** The temporary `child.once("error")` listener used during spawn validation is never removed after success. If a later runtime `error` event occurs, it still runs `processes.delete(handleId)`, so a running process disappears from the map and subsequent `sendMessage`/`destroy` calls fail with “No process found”.
Additional Locations (1) - [`packages/plugins/runtime-process/src/index.ts#L94-L95`](https://github.com/ComposioHQ/agent-orchestrator/blob/16d7efb873c138fc04b50c31a3455233ac239429/packages/plugins/runtime-process/src/index.ts#L94-L95)

### Worktree listing mixes similarly prefixed project IDs **Medium Severity** `list` filters entries with `path.startsWith(projectWorktreeDir)`, which also matches sibling directories that share the same prefix. Projects like `foo` and `foobar` can leak worktrees into each other’s results, returning incorrect `WorkspaceInfo` entries for the requested project.

### Concurrent tmux sends can paste wrong message **High Severity** Long-message delivery uses `load-buffer` and `paste-buffer` without a per-send buffer name. The default tmux buffer is shared, so concurrent `sendMessage` calls can overwrite each other between those two commands and paste the wrong content into a session.

### Symlink path can delete arbitrary filesystem paths **High Severity** `postCreate` trusts entries in `project.symlinks` and directly builds `targetPath` with `join`. Absolute or traversal values can resolve outside `info.path`, and the pre-symlink cleanup runs `rmSync` on that resolved path, allowing unintended deletion outside the workspace.

 

Triggered by project rule: BugBot Configuration

### Worktree removal prints success regardless of outcome **Low Severity** In `killSession`, the `git()` wrapper catches all errors and returns `null`, but the "Removed worktree" success message on the next line prints unconditionally. This contrasts with the tmux kill just above (lines 18–21), which correctly checks `killed !== null` before printing. Failed worktree removals will appear successful, potentially causing orphaned worktrees to accumulate without the user knowing.

### JSON output mode mixes decorative text with JSON **Medium Severity** When `--json` is passed, the banner (line 195), per-project headers (line 205), and footer summary (lines 231–236) are still printed as decorative text around the JSON arrays. This makes the output completely unparseable by `jq` or any JSON consumer. The `opts.json` flag only controls the per-project session rendering but doesn't suppress the surrounding non-JSON text.

### Missing error handler on browser-open spawn crashes dashboard **High Severity** The `spawn("open", ...)` call on line 83 has no `error` event listener. On non-macOS systems (Linux, Windows) where the `open` command doesn't exist, `spawn` emits an `ENOENT` `error` event. Per Node.js EventEmitter semantics, an unhandled `error` event throws and crashes the process — killing the running Next.js dashboard ~3 seconds after startup. This is the default behavior (`opts.open` is `true` unless `--no-open` is passed).

### Spinner never stopped when spawnSession throws mid-execution **Medium Severity** The `ora` spinner started on line 41 is never cleaned up if `spawnSession` throws (e.g., when `exec("tmux", ["new-session", ...])` fails on line 105). The spinner's internal `setInterval` keeps running. In `batch-spawn`, the error is caught on line 262 and the loop continues, so each failed spawn accumulates an orphaned spinner — garbling all subsequent terminal output and leaking timers.

### Stale errors in capture window misclassify idle as blocked **Medium Severity** The `detectActivity` method captures the last 15 lines of the tmux pane (`-S -15`) and checks patterns against the entire buffer. Since `BLOCKED_PATTERNS` is tested before `IDLE_PATTERNS`, a stale error message from earlier in the buffer (e.g., `Error: module not found`) will cause the agent to be classified as `"blocked"` even when it has recovered and is currently at an idle prompt (`❯`). The tests only verify "active overrides blocked" (line 471 of test file) but never test the "blocked + idle" co-occurrence, which will misclassify the agent and could trigger unnecessary lifecycle interventions.
Additional Locations (1) - [`packages/plugins/agent-claude-code/src/index.ts#L369-L372`](https://github.com/ComposioHQ/agent-orchestrator/blob/e285f62df8a0842703b85d97286294e147aeddec/packages/plugins/agent-claude-code/src/index.ts#L369-L372)

### Web build failures no longer fail CI **High Severity** The `typecheck` job now ignores failures from `pnpm --filter @agent-orchestrator/web build` via `|| true`, so CI can pass even when the web app has real build or type errors. This removes CI protection for `@agent-orchestrator/web` while comments still state web is typechecked there.

### Draft PRs misclassified into warning attention zone **Medium Severity** `getAttentionLevel` doesn't consider `pr.isDraft` when evaluating PR review state. A draft PR typically has `reviewDecision: "none"`, which triggers the warning-zone return on line 194. This causes actively-working sessions with draft PRs (like `frontend-6` in mock data, explicitly commented as "OK") to appear in the WARNING zone instead of the OK/WORKING zone.

This is by design and inherent to the process runtime model. Unlike tmux sessions which persist independently, child processes spawned via `spawn()` are tied to the orchestrator's process tree. When the orchestrator restarts, those child processes are gone (or orphaned by the OS) — there is no way to "reconnect" to an arbitrary `ChildProcess` by PID after restart.

This is exactly why the tmux runtime exists as the default: tmux sessions survive orchestrator restarts and can be reattached. The process runtime is intended for short-lived, ephemeral workloads where persistence across restarts is not needed.

The `RuntimeHandle.data.pid` field is available for callers that need to implement external cleanup (e.g., `kill <pid>`), but reconnection is not possible at the Node.js `ChildProcess` API level.

**Problem:** The `model` field was added to `SessionMetadata` type and set during `spawn()`, but `writeMetadata()` and `readMetadata()` were never updated to actually serialize/deserialize it. 1. **In readMetadata()** (line 95):
```typescript
model: raw["model"],
```

2. **In writeMetadata()** (line 136):
```typescript
if (metadata.model) data["model"] = metadata.model;
```

Now the model field is properly persisted to disk during spawn and correctly restored from metadata, eliminating reliance on project config fallback.

### Suffix matching resolves to wrong tmux session **High Severity** The `endsWith("-{sessionId}")` suffix match in `resolveTmuxSession` is ambiguous and can connect users to the wrong terminal session. The API contract in `AgentLaunchConfig` states that `systemPromptFile` "takes precedence over systemPrompt" when set, meaning `systemPrompt` should be ignored. Both `agent-aider` and `agent-claude-code` implement this correctly using `else if` to ensure mutual exclusion. The Cline plugin uses separate `if` statements, causing both to be concatenated into the final prompt, which violates the documented behavior and could lead to duplicate or conflicting system prompts being passed to the agent.

### Missing validation allows NaN PID return **Medium Severity** The `parseInt(cols[0] ?? "0", 10)` call on line 244 lacks validation to ensure it returns a valid number. If the PID column in `ps` output is malformed or non-numeric, `parseInt` returns `NaN`. Since `NaN !== null` evaluates to `true`, the `isProcessRunning` method incorrectly returns `true` for a non-existent process. This causes the orchestrator to believe an agent is running when it has actually terminated or never started, preventing proper cleanup and session state transitions. The function should validate the parsed result with `Number.isFinite()` before returning, similar to the validation on line 253 for the process runtime path.

### sessionFileMatchesCwd reads entire file despite documentation **Medium Severity** `sessionFileMatchesCwd` reads the entire file into memory but documentation claims it reads only the first 4KB. This causes unnecessary memory usage and I/O when scanning for matching session files, especially problematic with large rollout files. The function only uses the first 10 lines but loads everything.

### Race condition in binary resolution **Low Severity** `postLaunchSetup` has a check-then-act race condition where concurrent calls can both see `resolvedBinary` as null and both execute `resolveCodexBinary()`, wasting resources by resolving the binary path multiple times.

### Concurrent connect calls cause process leak **High Severity** `connect()` has a check-then-act race condition where concurrent calls spawn multiple processes. The second spawn overwrites `this.process`, orphaning the first process with no way to kill it. This causes a resource leak of child processes that continue running indefinitely.

### connect failure leaves resources uncleaned **Medium Severity** If `initialize()` throws during `connect()`, the spawned process and readline interface are left running without cleanup. The caller must explicitly call `close()` after a failed `connect()`, which is non-intuitive and error-prone.

### readline interface not closed on process exit **Medium Severity** `handleProcessExit` and `handleProcessError` don't close the readline interface, leaving it attached to the closed stdout stream. This resource leak prevents proper cleanup when the process exits unexpectedly, keeping event listeners active indefinitely.

### stderr pipe not consumed causes child blocking **High Severity** The spawned process pipes stderr but never consumes it. If the `codex app-server` writes enough to stderr, the buffer fills and the child process blocks waiting for the pipe to drain, causing the client to hang indefinitely.

### Binary resolve guard gets stuck on rejection **Medium Severity** `postLaunchSetup()` caches the in-flight `resolveCodexBinary()` promise in `resolvingBinary`, but if `resolveCodexBinary()` rejects, the code never clears `resolvingBinary`. Later calls keep awaiting the same rejected promise, so binary resolution can never recover within that agent instance.

### Merge steward merge may fail in detached worktree **Medium Severity** When `mergeMethod` is `"merge"`, the merge uses `options.sourceBranch` directly. The merge is discarded, yet the function returns `{ merged: true, tempWorktreePath }` with a path that no longer exists. Callers are told the merge succeeded even though nothing was persisted.

The `gh pr create` matcher requires `([[:space:]]|$)` after `create`, so a chained command like `gh pr create; ...` or `gh pr create&& ...` (no space) will no longer match. If the goal is to support command chaining with `;`, `&`, and `&&`, consider allowing those delimiters (or a general non-word boundary) after `create` rather than only whitespace/end-of-string.
```suggestion
if [[ "$command" =~ (^|[;&][[:space:]]*|&&[[:space:]]*)gh[[:space:]]+pr[[:space:]]+create([[:space:];&]|$) ]]; then
```

The `git checkout -b` pattern captures the branch with `([^[:space:]]+)`. With the newly-supported `;` / `&` chaining, a command like `git checkout -b foo; gh ...` (no space before `;`) will capture `foo;` as the branch. Consider excluding common command delimiters from the capture group and/or adding a post-branch boundary so separators aren’t included in the branch value.

Same issue as above for `git switch -c`: `([^[:space:]]+)` can capture delimiters when chaining without spaces (e.g. `git switch -c foo&& gh ...`), leading to an incorrect `branch` metadata value. Tighten the capture group and/or require a delimiter/whitespace boundary after the branch name.

The `git checkout <branch>` matcher can also capture trailing command delimiters when chaining without spaces (e.g. `git checkout feature/foo; ...`), since the branch group doesn’t stop at `;`/`&`. Consider stopping the capture at common separators and/or adding an explicit boundary after the branch token.

The `gh pr merge` matcher has the same `([[:space:]]|$)` suffix as `gh pr create`, which will fail to match chained invocations like `gh pr merge; ...` or `gh pr merge&& ...` without a space. If chaining delimiters are intended to be supported, allow `;`/`&`/`&&` as valid terminators here too.
```suggestion
if [[ "$command" =~ (^|[;&][[:space:]]*|&&[[:space:]]*)gh[[:space:]]+pr[[:space:]]+merge([[:space:];&]|$) ]]; then
```

Same delimiter-capture risk applies to the `git switch <branch>` matcher: without an explicit boundary after the branch token, chaining like `git switch feature/foo&& ...` can include `&&` in the captured branch. Adjust the capture/boundary to stop at common separators (`;`, `&`, `&&`, etc.).

### Shell syntax error: semicolon after `then` keyword **High Severity** The array of shell command fragments is joined with `"; "`, which places a semicolon immediately after the `then` keyword in the `if/then/fi` construct, producing `if [ -z "$SES_ID" ]; then; SES_ID=$(...)`. ### Stale fetch can overwrite state after project switch **Medium Severity** When the user switches projects, the EventSource effect cleanup closes the old connection but does not cancel the in-flight `fetch` triggered by a membership mismatch. The pending `fetch` carries the old `project` value in its closure. If it resolves *after* the new project's `initialSessions` reset, its `dispatch({ type: "reset" })` overwrites the state with stale sessions from the wrong project. **Root cause:** the eager `upsertReview` recorded the newly-resolved harness *before* the `len(created)==0` early return. So a harness switch on a trigger that creates no run persisted the new harness while the old pane kept running — and the next trigger read that back as `prevHarness`, so `prevHarness == harness` passed and `Notify` went to the stale old-harness pane. The DB's recorded harness had drifted from what the live pane was actually running.

**Fix:** the eager upsert only needs the review row to exist so the runs can reference it — it shouldn't advance the recorded harness ahead of an actual respawn. It now preserves an existing row's harness, and the harness only advances at the post-spawn upsert, after a real `Spawn`/`Notify`. That keeps the invariant *recorded harness == live pane's harness*, so the changed-harness respawn fires correctly on the next commit. It also tightens `Cancel`, which reads `review.Harness` and would previously have cancelled with the prematurely-advanced value.

**Tests:**
- `TestTriggerKeepsHarnessWhenNothingCreated` — the no-created trigger must not advance the recorded harness.
- `TestTriggerRespawnsOnNextCommitAfterHarnessSwitchWithNoRun` — the two-trigger sequence from your review: switch-with-no-run, then a new commit must respawn under the new harness, not `Notify` the stale pane.

Both fail on the old code and pass on the fix.

`restart` prints the same success line whether or not a review actually restarted.

The trigger controller distinguishes the two cases (controllers/reviews.go:105-107):

```go

// commit was reused.
status := http.StatusOK
if res.Created { status = http.StatusCreated }
```

But `TriggerReviewResponse` carries no `Created` field, so that distinction lives **only** in the status code — and `postJSON` -> `doJSONPath` throws the status away for any 2xx. So this line prints `triggered review for X` identically in both cases.

That's the exact workflow this command exists for. The PR's Problem section says the motivation is a run that got stuck or needs re-running, and in that case re-triggering on the same commit reuses the existing run and reports a fresh pass that never started. Silent and misleading.

Two ways out, either is fine:

- Cheap: soften the wording so it doesn't claim more than it knows, e.g. `requested review for %s`.
- Better: have the client surface the status code for this call so `restart` can say `started a new review pass` vs `reusing the in-flight run for this commit`. That's the information a user re-running a stuck review actually wants.

`res` is decoded and then never read, here and again at line 225 in `restartReview`.

```go
if err := c.postJSON(cmd.Context(), path, struct{}{}, nil); err != nil {

```

Relaxing `!chord.shift` here doesn't do anything, because line 120 rejects the event before it gets this far.

`app-shortcuts.ts:54` builds the chord from Electron's `input.key`, which follows `KeyboardEvent.key` semantics — the **shift-adjusted character**. On a US layout `Ctrl+Shift+backtick` delivers `key === "~"`, not `` ` ``. So line 120's `chord.key !== "`"` check throws it out.

I ran the real values through the function as it stands on this branch:

```
{ key: "~", ctrl: true, shift: true }  ->  false    // what Ctrl+Shift+` actually produces
{ key: "`", ctrl: true }               ->  true     // Ctrl+` still works, unchanged
{ key: "`", ctrl: true, shift: true }  ->  true     // what the new tests assert
```

The last row is the problem: the tests synthesize a `shift: true` chord that still carries the *unshifted* character, and the runtime can't produce that. So the suite goes green while the feature is inert.

Net effect of the PR as it stands: `Ctrl+`` keeps working exactly as before, `Ctrl+Shift+`` does nothing, and the catalog entry plus the topbar tooltip now both advertise `Ctrl+Shift+`` and no longer mention the chord that actually works. That's a step back from the current behavior.

The `"Backquote"` fallback on line 120 has the same root cause — `input.key` is never a `code` value, so that branch is unreachable in production and the test at shortcuts.test.ts:59 covers a path nothing can hit. `"Backquote"` is what `input.code` returns.

One fix covers both. Add `code` to `ShortcutChord`, pass `input.code` through in `app-shortcuts.ts`, and key off the physical code:

```ts
if (chord.code !== "Backquote") return false;
return chord.ctrl && !chord.meta && !chord.alt;
```

That gets you Shift-independence for free, and it also fixes the case your original comment was reaching for: layouts where backtick isn't a plain unmodified key. `code` is layout-independent, `key` isn't.

Worth checking whether `matchesNewSessionShortcut` and `matchesKeyboardShortcutsHelpShortcut` have the same latent issue — `⌘/` and `Ctrl+/` are unshifted so they're fine today, but the same `key`-vs-`code` trap applies to anything punctuation-based.

These caps can't do what the comment above them claims, because they run after the entire body is already in memory.

`decodeJSON` is just `json.NewDecoder(r.Body).Decode(out)` (projects.go:139), and there's no `http.MaxBytesReader` guarding it. I grepped the whole `backend/` tree for `MaxBytesReader` and there are zero hits, so nothing upstream is bounding the body either.

So the actual ordering in `spawn` is:

1. line 138 — fully materialize an arbitrary-size JSON body into `SpawnSessionRequest`, including base64 strings of unbounded length
2. line 162 — *then* check that the decoded attachments are under 25 MiB

By the time `decodeSpawnAttachments` can reject anything, the allocation has already happened. There's amplification too: the base64 string stays live while `base64.StdEncoding.DecodeString` allocates the decoded copy alongside it, so peak is roughly 1.75x the body.

This matters more than it would for a pure loopback daemon, since the LAN listener that serves AO Mobile reaches the same route.

One line before the decode fixes it:

```go
// Bound the body before decoding: the attachment caps below only apply once
// the payload is already in memory. 25 MiB decoded is ~34 MiB of base64, plus
// JSON overhead.
const maxSpawnBodyBytes = 40 << 20
r.Body = http.MaxBytesReader(w, r.Body, maxSpawnBodyBytes)
```

Worth a passing thought on whether the other `decodeJSON` call sites in this file want the same treatment, though none of the others carry inline payloads so they're much less exposed.

This test never exercises the max-age path it's named for.

`newTestObserver` pins the clock with `func() time.Time { return now }` (observer_test.go:229), so the second `Poll` sees the *identical* timestamp as the first. Setting `LastPRFetchAt = now` here means `now.Sub(last)` is exactly zero on the next poll.

So across both halves, the coverage is:

- part 1 — `LastPRFetchAt` empty, which takes the `last.IsZero()` branch at observer.go:864. That's the never-fetched case.
- part 2 — elapsed time of zero, asserting no refetch.

`now.Sub(last) > DefaultPRMaxAge` is never evaluated with a non-zero duration, so the headline behaviour of the PR — force a refetch once the snapshot is older than five minutes — has no coverage at all. Both halves would still pass if that comparison were deleted and replaced with `last.IsZero()`.

No clock plumbing needed to fix it, just backdate the cache entry:

```go
// Older than DefaultPRMaxAge: the forced refetch should fire even though
// both guards still report NotModified.
obs.Cache.LastPRFetchAt[prKey(testRepo, 1)] = now.Add(-6 * time.Minute)
```

and assert one fetch batch. Keeping the existing zero-elapsed case alongside it is worth doing too — together they'd actually pin the boundary.

Worth making the rate-limit trade explicit here, since it's the thing the ETag design was buying.

GitHub doesn't count `304 Not Modified` responses against the primary rate limit — that's most of the point of the conditional-request path this bypasses. With `DefaultTickInterval` at 30s and `DefaultPRMaxAge` at 5 minutes, every tracked open PR now forces one unconditional fetch every five minutes: 12/hour/PR that previously cost nothing. Across a fleet of 20 open PRs that's roughly 240 billable requests/hour against a 5000/hour authenticated budget.

Comfortable in isolation, but it scales linearly with the number of tracked PRs, which is the dimension AO is built to grow along. A user running 50+ sessions is in noticeably different territory, and secondary rate limits react to burstiness as much as volume — note this fires for all stale PRs in the same tick rather than being spread out.

Not arguing against the change, just that the constant deserves a comment recording the trade, and possibly a config knob rather than a hard-coded 5 minutes. If the root-cause question above resolves toward fixing the guard instead, this cost mostly goes away.

This only helps sessions spawned after the upgrade, which I don't think is enough to close #2608.

`repoPathForInfo` in the gitworktree adapter (adapters/workspace/gitworktree/workspace.go:874-885) treats `RepoPath` as an override with a fallback:

```go
if info.RepoPath != "" {
    return physicalAbs(info.RepoPath)   // the new path
}
if info.ProjectID == "" { ... }
return w.repoPath(info.ProjectID)       // the old path — the one that fails
```

That fallback is exactly why this change is safe, and also why it doesn't reach anything that already exists. Every session already in the database has an empty `Metadata.WorkspaceRepoPath`, so it takes the second branch and hits the same resolver lookup that fails for archived projects.

So the orphaned worktrees that motivated the issue stay orphaned. And the sessions this *does* protect are the newly-spawned ones, whose projects are the least likely to have been archived yet — the coverage is inverted relative to where the problem actually bites.

A one-time backfill on daemon boot would close it: for any session with an empty `WorkspaceRepoPath` whose project still resolves, resolve once and persist. Capturing the path while it's still resolvable is the whole point, since archiving happens later. `Reconcile` already walks sessions at boot, so there's a natural home for it.

If you'd rather keep this PR to the forward-looking half, that's reasonable — but then #2608 probably shouldn't be closed by it, and the backfill wants its own issue so the reporter's existing worktrees don't get forgotten.

Calling this directly breaks an invariant the rest of the file leans on.

`measureAndSend` opens with `frameRef.current = null` (line 140). That line reads as bookkeeping written on the assumption it's only ever reached *from inside* the rAF callback, where the handle has already fired. Invoking it directly here breaks that assumption, because a scheduled frame may still be pending.

Two things depend on `frameRef` being truthful:

```ts
const scheduleMeasure = useCallback(() => {
    if (frameRef.current !== null) return;   // line 175 — dedupe guard
```
```ts
const cancelScheduledMeasure = useCallback(() => {
    if (frameRef.current === null) return;   // line 166
    cancelAnimationFrame(frameRef.current);
```

So once a direct `measureAndSend()` nulls the handle mid-flight:

1. `scheduleMeasure()` will happily stack a **second** rAF while the first is still queued — the dedupe quietly stops working. That's under rapid toggling, which is exactly the scenario this PR targets.
2. `cancelScheduledMeasure()` at line 389 (the resize/scroll effect's cleanup) becomes a no-op for that orphaned frame, so it fires after teardown.

The blast radius is genuinely small — `measureAndSend` guards on `!node.isConnected` and falls through to `sendHiddenBounds`, so this is redundant IPC rather than wrong geometry. But a cancel that silently fails to cancel tends to get debugged expensively much later, and it's the same class of timing bug this PR exists to kill.

One line covers it:

```ts
cancelScheduledMeasure();
measureAndSend();
```

(`cancelScheduledMeasure` would need adding to the effect's dep array.) Alternatively, have `measureAndSend` cancel a live handle rather than blindly nulling it, which fixes it for every future direct caller too — probably the better shape given you've just established that direct calls are a legitimate pattern here.

Goose tracks applied migrations by **number, not by name**. Any database already at version 26 or higher sees 26 as done and skips this file without a word.

This is not theoretical, it happened on my machine tonight. My `goose_db_version` was at 27, stamped 2026-07-22 19:49 while I was on `main`. Running this branch afterwards left the old constraint in place:

```
CREATE TABLE projects (... kind TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'single_repo'
    CHECK (kind IN ('single_repo', 'workspace')))
```

So `UpsertProject` in `EnsureDefaultScratchProject` violates the CHECK, and the daemon does not degrade gracefully, it dies:


The app would not start at all until I hand-applied this migration's SQL. That will hit every existing user whose registry is empty at upgrade time, and the failure mode is a crash rather than a missing feature.

Fresh installs work fine because they run every migration in order, which is why all 12 checks are green. CI only ever creates new databases, so it structurally cannot catch this.

This gate makes deleting Scratch permanent, and the resulting state is the exact one the feature exists to prevent.

Removing a project archives the row rather than deleting it. The count here deliberately includes archived rows, so after someone deletes Scratch the count stays at 1 forever and this returns early on every subsequent boot. Scratch never comes back.

If that was the user's only project, they are left with zero live projects and an import screen offering Workspace or Project, both of which need a Git repo. That is precisely the wall Scratch was added to remove, and the product has no way out of it.

I hit this by accident within about ten minutes of normal use, and deleting an unfamiliar pre-made item is close to the first thing a lot of people try.

The rule is right for the case it was written for: someone adds their own real project, deletes Scratch, and does not want it reappearing. It is wrong when archiving Scratch leaves the registry empty. Gating on live non-scratch projects rather than any row that has ever existed keeps the intended behaviour and closes the trap, roughly "reseed when the only rows are archived scratch rows".

Related and much smaller: Scratch looks identical to a user-created project in the sidebar, with nothing marking it as built-in. That is part of why deleting it feels safe. And sessions land under the data dir at `<data>/scratch/default`, which nothing in the UI surfaces, so "where did my files go" is going to be a common first question.

Not blocking, but scratch is the worst case for this listing path and it is more expensive than it looks.

Two things:

**The walk never stops early.** On hitting the cap this sets `truncated` and returns `nil`, so `WalkDir` keeps traversing the whole tree. Every remaining entry still gets a `scratchWorkspaceFileInfo` stat. The only early exit in the file is the `SkipDir` for `.git` at line 234, and there is no `filepath.SkipAll`.

**Every file under the cap gets read in full.** `readWorkspaceTextFile(fullPath, maxWorkspaceFileBytes)` pulls up to 256KB per file purely so `textLineCount` can fill in `additions` for a listing. That is up to 5000 files read to render a file list.

For a git-backed project the equivalent numbers come from diff stats against the base. A scratch workspace is a bare directory an agent writes into freely, so one `npm install` and this walks and reads a `node_modules`. The surface that looks cheapest has the heaviest worst case.

`filepath.SkipAll` when the cap is reached is a one-liner. Deferring the line count to the file-detail endpoint, where a single file is already being read, is the larger win.

Two things I looked at and think are fine as they are: skipping `.git` inside a supposedly non-git directory is correct defensiveness since an agent may well run `git init`, and marking every file `WorkspaceFileAdded` is a reasonable modelling choice when there is no base to diff against.

`strings.ToLower` on the alias before resolution breaks case-sensitive lookup. OpenSSH `Host` patterns are case-sensitive, so an alias configured as `Host GitHub-Work` will not match after being lowercased to `github-work`, and `ssh -G github-work` returns the alias itself as hostname (no match), so resolution silently fails for any mixed-case alias. Your test `scp ssh alias` does not catch this because its injected resolver ignores the host argument. #2963/#2965 keep original casing for the resolver and lowercase only for the GitHub-host comparison and the normalized key.

This caches failures too (`ok=false` is stored), so a transient `ssh -G` failure (timeout, ssh briefly unavailable) is cached for the lifetime of the Provider and never retried. A GitHub-backed alias then stays unresolved until the daemon restarts. This is exactly the sticky negative cache #2965 calls out and fixes by not caching failures, letting the next observer poll recover.

`ssh -G host` runs without a `--` terminator and there is no guard rejecting hosts that start with `-`. A remote such as `git@-oProxyCommand=...:owner/repo` reaches here as host `-oProxyCommand=...` and ssh parses it as an option (argument injection from a remote URL). #2963/#2965 reject leading-dash hosts in both `resolveSSHHost` and `resolveSSHConfigHost` and pass `ssh -G -- host`. Worth adopting.

The not-caching-failures behavior is correct for transient errors. One consequence to be aware of: a host that genuinely errors on every `ssh -G` (for example ssh binary missing) will re-shell-out with the 1s timeout on every observer poll for that remote, since nothing is cached. In practice `ssh -G alias` succeeds even with no matching Host block (it echoes the alias back as hostname), so that success path does get cached and the repeated shell-out only affects true ssh failures. Acceptable tradeoff, just worth a comment so it is not mistaken for a leak.

The `--` plus leading-dash rejection is the right hardening. Note a shared limitation with #2957/#2965 (not introduced here): only the `git@`-prefixed scp form and `ssh://` URL form are resolved. An scp remote without the `git@` user (for example `work:owner/repo`, valid when ssh_config sets `User`) skips the git@ branch and is not alias-resolved. Fine to leave for a follow-up, but flagging in case such remotes are expected.

Good: keeping original casing here and only lowercasing for the GitHub-host comparison and normalized key is exactly what fixes #2957's case bug. The double-checked-locking on cache re-read after the resolver call (checking `p.sshHosts[host]` again under lock) also correctly collapses concurrent first-time lookups. No change requested.

The `ssh -G -- host` plus leading-dash rejection in both `resolveSSHHost` and here is the correct hardening. One shared limitation with #2957/#2963 (not introduced by this PR): only `git@`-prefixed scp remotes and `ssh://` URLs get alias resolution; an scp remote without the `git@` user (for example `work:owner/repo` relying on ssh_config `User`) is not resolved. Fine as a follow-up if such remotes matter.

If an operator splits the window (this is an inspectable keep-alive shell), the active pane at probe time may differ from the agent's pane and the read could miss the marker, reporting a dead agent as alive. All sessions share this promise chain, and it is not reset when the socket closes. A long `wait` blocks commands for every worker; commands whose HTTP caller timed out remain queued and can execute after reconnect, with their result written to the new socket. `Get` only proves that the supplied session exists. The caller chooses `sessionId`, and `AO_SESSION_ID` is mutable client-side state, so any loopback caller can issue screenshot, click, or get commands against another worker; terminated sessions also pass this check. `clear` only blanks the active tab. It leaves every other tab, the session partition, and any active network capture alive. Because session termination calls this path rather than `destroy`, ending a session does not dispose its browser state. Termination must destroy all tabs and captures and invalidate the session target.

**Main finding — an empty manager path can preserve a project-supplied `AO_RUN_FILE`.**

`projectEnv` is copied into `env` before this conditional. For example:

```go
projectEnv := map[string]string{EnvRunFile: "/wrong"}
env := spawnEnv("s-1", "p", "", "/data", "", projectEnv)
```

Because `runFilePath == ""`, this branch does nothing, so the result still contains:

```go
env[EnvRunFile] == "/wrong"
```

For example, suppose a configured integration gate takes 90 seconds while the HTTP middleware times out after 60 seconds. The gate continues, persists the fused verdict, and then this call starts with an already-canceled context. A context-aware store or lifecycle operation can fail, leaving the review complete with a fused verdict but undelivered to the worker.

Please give gate plus delivery one durable owner: either persist/resume the whole operation as a job, or carry one service-owned context through both phases. A regression test should use context-aware store/lifecycle fakes and cancel the request while the gate is running.

Measured against real git 2.54 before choosing it:

Confirmed against real git 2.54, exactly as you describe: `git worktree add -b newbr <stale-path> main` prints "Preparing worktree (new branch 'newbr')", exits 128 on the missing-registration check, and `show-ref --verify refs/heads/newbr` then resolves. The `--force -b` retry exits 255 with `fatal: a branch named 'newbr' already exists`. So the recovery never recovered.

Fixed in c7d79f3, both halves you suggested:

1. **Retry on the existing-branch form.** The retry is now `git worktree add --force <path> <branch>` when `refs/heads/<branch>` resolves after the failed attempt (measured: it recovers the stale path and leaves the worktree checked out on that branch at the requested base). The ref is re-read rather than assumed, so a caller that does not guarantee the branch was absent beforehand still gets the right form. The `-b` form is kept for the case where the ref is genuinely not there.

2. **Detect the stale registration before the first attempt.** `createWorkspaceProjectRepo` now does the same `worktree list` pre-check `addWorktree` already had, so the ordinary #2775 shape is handled by the very first add carrying `--force` and never creates a stray ref at all. The retry is now only reachable when the registration goes stale after that check.

Both call sites go through one helper, `addNewBranchWorktree`, so the two retry shapes cannot drift apart again.

On the leftover ref when recovery fails outright: I left it in place deliberately rather than deleting it. The failure that gets you there is `fatal: '<path>' already exists` (non-empty directory), which means something else materialized the worktree at that path first, possibly checked out on this very branch, so deleting the ref would damage the worktree that won the race. It is also self-correcting: the next `addWorktree` for that branch takes the existing-branch path, and `workspaceProjectBranch` just picks the next free candidate. Reasoning is in the helper's doc comment.

- The fake test is split in two and now models the failed `-b` invocation's branch-creation side effect instead of treating it as side-effect-free: `TestCreateWorkspaceProjectRepoAddsWithForceWhenRegistrationIsStale` covers the pre-check path (one add, no retry), and `TestCreateWorkspaceProjectRepoRecoveryRetriesOnExistingBranchForm` covers the recovery, asserting the retry uses the existing-branch form and that the `-b` form is not repeated. **Base ref candidate order is inverted relative to how the worktree was actually created.**

`gitworktree.baseRefCandidates` (`commands.go:131`) deliberately puts `origin/<default>` **before** `refs/heads/<default>`, and says so in a comment: *"The local head comes after origin/<defaultBranch> so remote-tracking still wins when present."* Its test pins the order: `["origin/feature/test", "origin/main", "refs/heads/main", "feature/test"]`.

So the worktree is created from `origin/main`, but this list resolves local `main` first, and `merge-base HEAD main` uses `refs/heads/main`. Whenever local `main` lags `origin/main` (the normal state, since nobody pulls `main` before every session) the recorded base is stale and the session reports upstream commits as its own work immediately on spawn, with no rebase involved.

Verified against a real clone with local `main` one commit behind:

```
local main : d96e0ec      origin/main : 2a18ab8

merge-base HEAD main         = d96e0ec  ->  A agent.txt  M shared.txt  A upstreamonly.txt
merge-base HEAD origin/main  = 2a18ab8  ->  A agent.txt
```

The agent only wrote `agent.txt`.

Suggested fix, move the local branch to last so this matches `gitworktree`:

```go
	if !strings.HasPrefix(defaultBranch, "origin/") && !strings.HasPrefix(defaultBranch, "refs/") {
		add("origin/" + defaultBranch)
		add("refs/remotes/origin/" + defaultBranch)
	}
	add(defaultBranch)
	return refs
```

**Same inverted ordering as `spawnDiffBaseRefCandidates`, so the read-time fallback repeats the bug.**

This list also resolves local `<defaultBranch>` before `origin/<defaultBranch>`, which contradicts `gitworktree.baseRefCandidates` (`commands.go:131`). Any session that reaches this fallback path with a stale local `main` gets a merge base behind the commit its worktree was actually created from.

Same fix: move `add(defaultBranch)` after the two `origin/` entries. Both lists need it, since one records the base and this one recovers it.

I applied both reorderings plus the `resolveWorkspaceCompare` change below and the full suite stayed green, including `internal/adapters/workspace/gitworktree` whose `TestBaseRefCandidates` pins the convention.

**This picks whichever PR was updated most recently, which is not a stable base.**

`ListPRsBySession` is `ORDER BY updated_at DESC` (`queries/pr.sql:88`), so `prs[0]` is just the last-touched PR. For a session with more than one PR (the multi-PR sessions from #2172) the comparison base can change on its own whenever PR update ordering changes, with no code or branch change. On a stacked session, picking a child PR's `BaseSHA` compares only against its parent and silently hides everything lower in the stack.

Prefer the root or default-target PR, or add an explicit `ORDER BY created_at ASC` for this use, rather than relying on `updated_at` ordering.

Minor, same block: this runs inside `resolveWorkspaceCompare`, which `listWorkspaceProjectFiles` calls once per child repo, so an N-repo workspace issues N identical queries plus N `cat-file` execs. Worth hoisting the PR lookup out of the per-repo loop.

**`git status` is relative to HEAD, `git diff <base>` is relative to base. Letting status win unconditionally makes the reported status describe the wrong baseline.**

Verified output from this code path, on a branch that committed two new files and then touched them in the worktree:

```
path=added_then_deleted.go    status=deleted    +0/-0
path=added_then_edited.go     status=modified   +3/-0
```

- `added_then_edited.go` was created in a branch commit then edited. It does not exist in base, so it is `added`, not `modified`. The `+3/-0` from numstat already says so, so the row contradicts its own counts.
- `added_then_deleted.go` was created in a branch commit then deleted uncommitted. Net effect versus base is nothing, but it renders as a phantom `deleted` row whose diff body comes back empty.

The underlying point is that `git diff <base>` with no `--cached` already covers committed, staged **and** unstaged changes, so `workspaceStatuses` is only genuinely needed for untracked entries. Restricting the merge to those lets diff-vs-base own tracked-file status and both cases above resolve:

```go
	for rel, status := range statusStatuses {
		if _, tracked := diffStatuses[rel]; tracked {
			continue // base-relative status already correct
		}
		statuses[rel] = status // untracked (??) only
	}
```

Renames followed by an edit are mislabeled the same way.

**The `maxWorkspaceFiles` cap is per repo, not global, so the guard is bypassed in multi-repo workspaces.**

Each call gets its own 5000 budget and results are appended with no aggregate check, while `truncated` is only OR'd across rows. Two child repos with 4000 files each return 8000 entries with `Truncated == false`, so both the response-size guard and the truncation signal to the client are defeated.

Thread the remaining budget through the loop and set `truncated` once the aggregate limit is hit, rather than capping each repo independently.

Note this interacts with the ordering issue on line 749: one bug drops changed files below the cap, the other lets the aggregate exceed it. A single budget-aware pass that prioritizes changed paths fixes both.

**One unresolvable child repo flips the whole response to `head_fallback`, contradicting the data that was already computed.**

If any single repo failed to resolve a base, this returns `head_fallback` with an empty SHA. But every repo's files were already diffed against **its own** resolved base at line 327, so the response metadata now describes something different from the file list it ships with. On the client that surfaces as `emptyFilesMessage` claiming "No changes against HEAD." for a set that was in fact compared against base.

Consider reporting per-repo compare state, or at least keeping `mode: base` when at least one repo resolved and signalling the partial failure separately.

**`defaultBranch` is being passed in the `recordedRef` parameter slot.**

The signature is `resolveWorkspaceCompare(ctx, rec, root, recordedSHA, recordedRef, defaultBranch)`, so this call sets `recordedRef = defaultBranch`. Child repos then report `CompareBaseRef` as the default branch name while `CompareBaseSHA` is `row.BaseSHA`, the worktree's creation SHA. Those are two different commits, so the API advertises provenance that does not match the SHA it returns.

Line 362 in `getWorkspaceProjectFile` does the same thing.

Either pass `""` for `recordedRef` and let the resolver label it, or record a real ref alongside `BaseSHA` on the worktree row.

The ordering you describe is real, but I don't think either stated consequence follows. Walking it through:

**On the mechanism** — correct. `onExit`/`onError` call `flushReplay()` and then `transition(...)`, and `showReplayCover` is gated on `connecting || attached`, so the state change drops the cover without waiting for xterm's write callback. Same on the reconnect path via `onConnectionChange("closed")` → `scheduleReattach()` → `reattaching`.

**"Briefly expose stale output"** — there is nothing stale to expose. While the gate is open nothing has been written to xterm yet, and that is the whole point of buffering. On a first attach xterm's buffer is empty; on a reattach `connect()` has already called `terminal.clear()` before arming the gate. So what shows for that frame is a blank grid, which is visually what the cover itself was showing (`bg-terminal`).

**"Reproduce the scrolling artifact"** — this one I'd push back on more firmly. The artifact needs *multiple* writes painting successive scroll positions. The flush is a single `write()` of the joined buffer, and xterm parses one write-buffer entry in one uninterrupted `_action` call — the 12ms yield check sits *between* entries, never inside one. So the flush can produce at most one paint regardless of when its callback fires (two on the exit path, since `writeln("[process exited]")` follows). One jump, never a walk.

So the net effect is the residual I noted in the review comment above: one blank frame is possible at the reveal, because the cover's removal goes through React state while xterm's paint goes through its own render scheduler. That's true on the happy path too, not just on exit/error, and it's blank rather than wrong.

**The part I think is a fair hit**: the fake does invoke `done` synchronously, so the suite genuinely does not exercise callback-after-state-change ordering. Happy to make it async — worth knowing before I do that it isn't a free change, because `onExit`/`onError` currently settle *through* that callback, so tests like `lands buffered output and lifts the cover when the pane exits mid-replay` assert `replaySettled` immediately after `emitExit()` and would need timer advances. That's arguably the suite becoming more honest. Want me to take it?

Concretely: the daemon dies mid-session and the supervisor publishes `{ state: "stopped", code: "exited" }` (`frontend/src/main.ts`). Reusing the shell's predicate fixes it, either by passing `isStartupLoading` down through the shell context or by applying the same `code` check here:

```ts
const daemonIsFailed = Boolean(shell?.daemonStatus.code);
const showStartup =
    shell !== null &&
    !daemonIsFailed &&
    (!isDaemonReady || workspaceStartupState === "loading" || (!workspaceQuery.isSuccess && !workspaceQuery.isError));
```

This overwrites the preference of anyone who deliberately keeps the sidebar collapsed.

`isSidebarOpen` is persisted: `toggleSidebar` writes to `localStorage` under `sidebarStorageKey` (`stores/ui-store.ts:176-178`), and `initialSidebarOpen()` reads it back at launch (`ui-store.ts:144`). So for a user whose saved preference is collapsed, every launch goes:

1. `isStartupLoading` is true, so `sidebarWasCollapsedForStartupRef` is set to true.
2. Startup finishes. The ref is true, and `isSidebarOpen` is `false` — that's their own saved preference, not something startup did.
3. `toggleSidebar()` fires, opens the sidebar, and writes `true` back to localStorage.

The preference is overwritten on disk rather than just for the session, so a collapsed sidebar can never stick across launches.

The root cause is that the ref's name doesn't match what actually happened: nothing collapsed the sidebar. Line 656 only overrides the `open` prop and leaves the store value untouched, so by the time this branch runs there's no way to tell "we hid it for startup" from "the user wants it hidden."

Since line 656 already reverts to `isSidebarOpen || isSidebarPeekOpen` the moment `isStartupLoading` goes false, the restore branch looks unnecessary — dropping lines 467-469 and the ref should give the intended behavior on its own. Two things about this comparison.

`dataUpdatedAt` is a `Date.now()` millisecond stamp, so if the confirmed fetch resolves within the same millisecond as the value already sitting in the cache, this returns early and the loader stays up until the next `refetchInterval` tick (15s) or an event-transport invalidation. Unlikely with two loopback GETs plus the JSON mapping, but the tests step 100 -> 200 and never exercise equality, so nothing would catch it if it did happen.

The larger point: this accepts *any* newer successful stamp, not specifically the fetch the effect above issued. That's correct today only because of two properties that live in other files:

1. `useDaemonStatus` calls `applyDaemonStatus` (which sets the base URL) before `setStatus`, so any refetch starting after the ready render is a real request.
2. The untrusted path in `fetchWorkspaces` is a bare `return []` with no `await` ahead of it, so a placeholder fetch resolves within a microtask and can't still be in flight for `queryClient.fetchQuery` to dedupe into. If it could, that call would resolve `[]`, stamp a newer `dataUpdatedAt`, and flip the state to `ready` with exactly the empty list this PR exists to distrust.

Add a single `await` before the trust check in `fetchWorkspaces` and the original bug comes back silently. Both new shell tests mock `fetchQuery` and `getQueryState`, so neither property is covered.

Cleanest fix is upstream: have `fetchWorkspaces` throw instead of returning `[]` when there's no trusted base URL, which removes the ambiguity this whole mechanism is working around. Failing that, a comment at both sites recording the dependency would at least make it survive the next refactor.

`fetchQuery` respects `staleTime`, and the shared client sets `staleTime: 10_000` (`lib/query-client.ts`). So on the exact path this effect exists to handle, it usually doesn't fetch anything.

Cold start: the route loader at line 49 runs `ensureQueryData` before a port is known, `fetchWorkspaces` returns `[]` through the `hasTrustedApiBaseUrl()` guard, and that lands in the cache at t~0. The daemon reports ready a second or two later, this effect runs, and the cached `[]` is still fresh — so `fetchQuery` returns it without contacting the daemon. `dataUpdatedAt` never moves, and the recovery effect's `dataUpdatedAt > baseline` test can't pass.

What actually unblocks the board today is the agent-catalog effect at line 499, which invalidates `workspaceQueryKey` at line 506 on the same `[daemonStatus.port, daemonStatus.state, queryClient]` change and forces a real refetch. That's an unrelated effect this gate is silently depending on.

And it doesn't always fire. Line 501 early-returns when `agentCatalogPortRef.current === daemonStatus.port`, so a daemon that restarts and comes back on the *same* port skips the invalidation — which is the normal case in dev, where `DEV_DAEMON_PORT` / `AO_PORT` are fixed. In that case this `fetchQuery` short-circuits on the still-fresh cache too, nothing advances `dataUpdatedAt`, and the loader sits until the 15s `refetchInterval` fires.

Opting out of `staleTime` here would make the confirmed fetch actually confirm something:

```ts
void queryClient
    .fetchQuery({ ...workspaceQueryOptions, staleTime: 0 })
    .catch(...)
```

**Teardown dead-end: a stale checkout makes `Destroy` fail forever, leaking the sandbox.**

`isDirty` maps a stale checkout (path gone / not a repo — e.g. the agent removed the dir, or a half-failed provision whose cleanup delete also failed) to an error, and `Destroy` returns it. The session manager kill path only special-cases `ErrWorkspaceDirty` (`manager.go:873`); an `ErrWorkspaceStale`-wrapped error falls into the generic `kill: workspace:` failure, and every retry fails identically because the checkout never comes back. Result: an unkillable session and a sandbox that keeps billing until auto-archive. The cleanup path (`manager.go:2156`) skips it forever for the same reason.

gitworktree succeeds in the analogous case (unregistered path → prune → removeAll → nil), and the comment here even says stale means nothing to protect — but the code returns the error instead of proceeding. Suggest: when the dirty probe fails with a definitive `execError` (stale), fall through to `deleteAndWait` rather than returning.

**Reuse path ignores `cfg.Branch`, so a retried provision can leave the session on the base branch.**

If a prior provision died after the clone but before the session-branch checkout (daemon crash — the delete-on-failure cleanup only runs when the failing Create call itself is still executing), this reuse path sees a valid repo and returns `currentBranch()`, i.e. the cloned base branch. The session then silently runs on the base branch and `WorkspaceInfo.Branch` records it as such — nasty to debug downstream (review/PR flows expect the session branch).

Suggest reconciling on reuse: when `cfg.Branch` is set and differs from the current branch, run the same fetch/checkout script as the fresh path.

**Two related hazards on this failure-cleanup path.**

(a) The `rev-parse --is-inside-work-tree` probe above treats *any* error — including toolbox transport failures like the 502s you observed live during state transitions — as not-provisioned. A transient failure against a healthy checkout then proceeds to `GitClone` into a non-empty dir, which fails.

(b) This cleanup then deletes the sandbox unconditionally, even when it was adopted (`found == true`) rather than created by this call.

Combined: a transient probe failure on a retried spawn deletes a sandbox holding a valid checkout — possibly with uncommitted work — without a stash. Narrow, but it is the one destructive path in the adapter. Suggest gating the provisioned-probe on a definitive `execError` (transport errors should abort inconclusively, matching the careful split everywhere else in this package), and only deleting sandboxes this Create call itself created.

**Fetch failure is conflated with branch-does-not-exist.**

`git fetch origin <branch>` also fails on auth and transient network errors — and for private repos (the primary cloud case per the custody model) the clone credentials traveled in the toolbox API body, so in-sandbox `git fetch` has no credentials at all unless the snapshot carries ambient ones. In those cases a restore/re-provision silently creates a fresh branch from base instead of resuming the remote session branch: prior work is still on the remote, but the session resumes from the wrong state with no signal.

Worth separating missing-ref from failed-fetch (e.g. `git ls-remote --exit-code origin refs/heads/<branch>` distinguishes exit 2 = absent from other failures), or at minimum failing hard when credentials were provided for the clone.

Minor inconsistency: this maps *any* exec failure — including toolbox transport errors — to `ErrWorkspaceStale`, whereas `StashUncommitted` (exit 3) and `isDirty` gate stale on a definitive `execError`. A transient toolbox hiccup during restore should surface as an inconclusive error, not report the checkout as stale.

Can we make this identity dependency explicit from the SCM wiring boundary instead of having the observer discover it through a provider type assertion? I think the behavior is right for auto-discovery: gate on AO’s active SCM identity, and if a PR was opened/pushed outside AO with a different GitHub account, require explicit `ao pr claim` rather than branch-name auto-attribution.

The change I’d like here is to wire a lazy/cached identity resolver alongside the SCM provider and have the observer use that dependency directly. That keeps daemon startup non-blocking, preserves the current fallback when identity is unavailable or bot/app-backed, and gives us one reusable source for “the GitHub account AO is authenticated as” across observer/doctor/future PR flows.

Addressed in e2d34eccf. I added a provider-neutral SCMIdentityResolver dependency and now inject it explicitly from daemon SCM wiring instead of discovering it through a provider type assertion.
